cues.text: Chapter six is exam consolidation, so think of this as your final checklist before the exam.
Let me walk through what you need to know, in the order the source gives it.
First, you must be able to distinguish quality assurance from quality control and testing.
Keep these apart in your mind.
Quality assurance, or QA, is the broader concern, while quality control and testing are the narrower activities that the source pairs together as the other side of that comparison.
Second, know the test levels.
These are the different stages or scopes at which software is tested, and you should be able to name them and say what each one covers.
Third, know the difference between functional and nonfunctional testing.
Functional testing asks whether the system does what it is supposed to do.
Nonfunctional testing looks at qualities of how it behaves.
Fourth, know black-box, white-box and grey-box testing.
These describe how much the tester knows about the internal workings of the system while testing it.
Fifth, know the boundary and decision-table techniques.
These are two named test design techniques, and you should be ready to apply each of them, not only define them.
Sixth, know the automation tools you have studied for testing.
Seventh, know TDD and BDD.
That is test-driven development and behaviour-driven development.
Be ready to explain each one and how they differ.
Eighth, know defect triage and root cause analysis.
Triage is about handling reported defects, and root cause analysis is about finding why a defect occurred.
Ninth, know test coverage, meaning how much of the software your tests actually exercise.
Tenth, know the limitations of AI automation in testing.
The source specifically lists this as something to be able to discuss, so be prepared to say where AI-driven automation falls short.
Now comes the central principle of the chapter, and it is worth remembering word for word in spirit: choose your testing strategy by real risk, not by the number of passing scripts.
A large count of passing automated scripts does not prove that the things that matter most are safe.
What matters is where the genuine risk lies, and your strategy should be built around that.
Finally, a note about your assessment.
The source says the submitted CA, the continuous assessment, is particularly rich in QA cases.
So when you revise, give extra attention to applying quality assurance ideas to realistic case situations, rather than only memorising definitions.
